t: Count Subarrays With More Ones Than Zeros - Prefix Sums and a Fenwick Tree
o: Map every 0 to -1 and a subarray has more ones than zeros exactly when its transformed sum is positive. In nums = [0,1,1,0,1] the nine winning subarrays break down as three singletons, one pair ([1,1]), three triples, one length-4 and the whole array. With n up to 10^5, inspecting all O(n^2) subarrays (about 10^10 candidates) is impossible, pointing toward prefix sums plus a counting structure. The count grows quickly, hence the 10^9 + 7 modulus.
k: Rewriting zeros as -1 turns "more ones than zeros" into "transformed sum is positive".
A subarray (i, j] has positive sum iff prefix[j] > prefix[i], so the answer is the number of index pairs i < j with prefix[i] < prefix[j].
A Fenwick tree over prefix values shifted by n answers "how many earlier prefixes are strictly below v" in O(log n) per step.

a.i: Fix a left endpoint and extend the right end while keeping the running balance of ones minus zeros; each moment the balance is positive marks one valid subarray. Simple and useful as a correctness reference, but quadratic.
s: For each start i, initialize bal = 0.
Extend j rightward, adding +1 for a 1 and -1 for a 0.
Add one to the answer whenever bal > 0.
a.t: O(n^2) - around 10^10 balance updates at n = 10^5; only usable on tiny inputs.

a.i: Let prefix[j] be the transformed sum of the first j elements, with prefix[0] = 0. A subarray ending at j is good iff some earlier prefix is strictly smaller, so a single left-to-right sweep that queries "prefixes stored so far that are below prefix[j]" counts everything. Transformed prefixes live in [-n, n]; shifting by n indexes a BIT of size 2n + 2. Each element costs one prefix-range query and one insertion.
s: Insert the shifted value of prefix[0] = 0 (that is, n) into the Fenwick tree.
Sweep j from 1 to n, keeping pref as the transformed running sum.
Add query(pref + n - 1) - the number of stored prefixes strictly below pref - to the answer modulo 1e9 + 7.
Insert pref + n into the tree.
Return the answer after the sweep.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def subarraysWithMoreOnesThanZeroes(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
        n = len(nums)
        size = 2 * n + 2
        tree = [0] * (size + 1)

        def update(i):
            i += 1
            while i <= size:
                tree[i] += 1
                i += i & (-i)

        def query(i):
            i += 1
            res = 0
            while i > 0:
                res += tree[i]
                i -= i & (-i)
            return res

        update(n)
        pref = 0
        ans = 0
        for x in nums:
            pref += 1 if x == 1 else -1
            ans = (ans + query(pref + n - 1)) % MOD
            update(pref + n)
        return ans

a.t: O(n log n) - one Fenwick query and one update per element.

w: Lead with the reduction: zeros to -1, then count prefix pairs i < j with prefix[i] < prefix[j]; interviewers grade the transformation more than the BIT mechanics. Watch the strict inequality - subarrays with equally many ones and zeros must not count - and apply the modulus at every addition. A merge-sort-based pair count or offline coordinate compression gives the same complexity. Likely follow-ups: report the count ending at each index, or handle streaming updates to the array.
